input: This worked example sets out to calculate the steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant in an esterification reaction carried out in a continuous stirred-tank reactor. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, which means that the rate is proportional to the concentration of that reactant, and the rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.021 min-1. The mean residence time in the vessel is 35 min; the mean residence time, it should be explained, is the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate, and it represents the average time that a fluid element spends in the vessel. Multiplying the rate constant by the mean residence time gives a product of 0.735. The conversion is the fraction of the limiting reactant that is converted at the outlet, stated against the feed concentration of that reactant. Because the rate falls as the reactant is consumed, the conversion is set by the balance between the reaction taking place in the vessel and the flow passing through it, and not by the inlet concentration acting on its own. For a first-order reaction at steady state in an ideal CSTR (continuous stirred-tank reactor), the conversion is given by this product divided by one plus this product, since the whole contents of the vessel sit at the exit concentration and the rate is everywhere the exit rate. Substituting the numbers gives a conversion of 42.4%. It is important to note that the estimate rests on the assumptions of perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the key assumption carrying the result: the exit-rate form holds only while the contents remain uniform. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so mixing in the vessel remains unchecked, and any dead volume or bypassing would move the conversion away from 42.4% while leaving the stated rate constant and residence time unchanged. The resulting figure is also bounded by construction: it sits below complete conversion, as a finite residence time at a finite rate necessarily requires.
